title: US Court Dispatches Summonses to Doval, Goel in Pannun Case via Delhi Courts
excerpt: The Southern District of New York sent the summonses by FedEx to the Patiala House, Tis Hazari and Dwarka courts under the Hague Convention, after service through India's central authority was attempted and rejected — a route New Delhi says is not lawful.
body:
• A US court clerk has dispatched summonses for National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and former R&AW chief Samant Goel by FedEx to three Delhi district courts — Patiala House, Tis Hazari and Dwarka — in Gurpatwant Singh Pannun's civil suit.
  • The dispatch follows a November 13 order by Judge Katherine Polk Failla authorising service through Indian courts under Article 19 of the Hague Convention and Section 29(c) of India's Code of Civil Procedure, after service through India's central authority was attempted and rejected.
  • India rejected the suit on November 10 as "fabricated and malicious" and says judicial documents can only be served through its designated central authority, the Ministry of Law and Justice.
  • The order decides only how summonses may be served. It makes no finding on Pannun's allegations, which have not been established in any court.

A US federal court has dispatched summonses to National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and former Research and Analysis Wing director Samant Goel through courts in Delhi, taking the next procedural step in the civil lawsuit filed by Khalistani separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun. The clerk of the Southern District of New York said the summonses were sent through FedEx to the Patiala House Court, the Tis Hazari Court and the Dwarka District Court in New Delhi on Friday, The Hindu BusinessLine reported.

What the court ordered

In an order dated November 13, US District Judge Katherine Polk Failla directed the court clerk to transmit the summonses and accompanying judicial documents to the Delhi courts under the Hague Convention on the Service Abroad of Judicial and Extrajudicial Documents. "The court respectfully requests the assistance of receiving Indian courts in effecting service of process upon the defendants in this civil action pending before this court," the order read. The Patiala House Court was asked to effect service on Doval, while the documents for Goel were sent to both the Dwarka and Tis Hazari courts, LawBeat reported.

The legal route matters. Section 29(c) of India's Code of Civil Procedure permits summonses issued by foreign civil courts designated by a central government notification to be transmitted to Indian courts and served as though issued by those courts. The US court recorded that standard service through India's central authority under Article 5 of the Hague Convention had been attempted and rejected, and it authorised the alternative route under Article 19, which allows a method permitted by the receiving country's own law. Each transmission was to include the summons, the court's order, the relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure and records showing the earlier attempted service.

"We reject the fabricated and malicious attacks on our high officials. Also, we reject the frivolous lawsuits."

— Randhir Jaiswal, Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson, November 10

India's objection

India has rejected both the suit and the service route. On November 10, External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said: "We reject the fabricated and malicious attacks on our high officials. Also, we reject the frivolous lawsuits. A request for serving of judicial documents in India can only be routed through India's designated central authority, which is the Ministry of Law and Justice." The dispute is therefore now two-layered: a procedural fight over how — and whether — the summonses can lawfully be served in India, ahead of any hearing on the claims themselves. The November 13 order followed an earlier November 9 ruling accepting Pannun's argument that Article 19 permits service through India's court system, and it followed unsuccessful attempts by Pannun's lawyers to serve Doval in person during his official visits to the United States.

The suit behind the summonses

Pannun, general counsel of the banned organisation Sikhs for Justice, filed the civil suit in September 2024 in the Southern District of New York. It names the Government of India, Doval, Goel, former Indian government employee Vikash Yadav, Nikhil Gupta and 50 unnamed defendants. Pannun alleges the defendants conspired to assassinate him at his home in New York in 2023 in retaliation for his advocacy of an independent Sikh state, and he is seeking damages. The allegations have not been established in the civil proceedings, and the latest order makes no finding on their merits or on any defendant's liability. The civil suit is distinct from the US Justice Department's criminal prosecution over the alleged murder-for-hire plot, in which Gupta pleaded guilty in February 2026 — a plea that, as LawBeat noted, does not establish the civil allegations against Doval, Goel or the Government of India. India has said Yadav was no longer a government employee as of October 2024 and constituted a committee to examine the evidence raised by US authorities.

What happens next

The Delhi courts have been asked to accept the documents, serve them under the procedures that apply to their own summonses, and return a written record of the proceedings to the US court clerk. Whether the Indian courts act on a request India says should never have bypassed its central authority is the immediate question — and the answer will decide whether Pannun's civil case can move from the service stage to a substantive hearing at all.
